genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist in mapping footpaths inspects the routes before the walking season
waymarks hold badly on steep rock faces
walkers lose the route when mist comes down
she measures the slope of the ground with a dedicated instrument
she sets a rod sealed with resin into hard rock
she chooses a weighted post in crumbling rock
each mark must be visible from the one before it
this method cuts down the number of rescue call-outs
she records the positions in a register read by the maintenance teams
text: Before the walking season opens, the woman who maps a footpath network goes out to inspect every route in turn. She knows the trouble well: waymarks hold badly on steep rock faces, and walkers stray off the line as soon as the mist comes down. So she measures the slope with a clinometer, notes what the rock is made of, and picks an anchor to match it. In hard, compact stone she sets a rod sealed with resin; in flaky, crumbling rock she prefers a weighted post that no frost will lift. Then she marks the way in short runs, placing each sign where the one before it can still be seen. The method cuts down the number of rescue call-outs and stops walkers turning back for no reason. Every position goes into a register, which the maintenance teams read through before they set off on their rounds.

units: two viewing platforms look out over the same valley
the upper platform is built on a rocky spur above the gorge
the upper platform is reached by very steep steps
the second platform lies lower down on a grassy shelf
the view from the lower platform is partly hidden by the rock wall
the lower approach suits groups with children better
a strong wind makes the upper platform unpleasant
the writer finally judges the lower platform more satisfying
the quality of a built facility depends on the fit between a place and its public
text: Two viewing platforms look out over the same valley, and they deserve very different verdicts. The higher one stands on a spur of rock above the gorge, and it makes you work for it: the steps are steep, the handrail narrow, and you arrive out of breath in front of a panorama that repays the climb. The lower one sits on a grassy shelf and costs almost nothing to reach, though what the view loses in sweep it gains in gentleness, since the rock wall hides part of it. You might favour the first for its harshness, the second for its kindness towards groups with children. Once the wind gets up, though, the comparison settles in favour of the lower one: the high platform turns unpleasant, while the sheltered ledge keeps its charm. What makes such a place work is less its height than the fit between the site and the people who come to it.

units: the writer is writing from lodgings set on a slope
the wind beats against the shutters of the house
the room is bare and the bed uncomfortable
the window looks out onto a dry expanse
meals include warm flatbreads and a very salty cheese
the drink served has a bitter taste
the walking starts at sunrise on tracks that wind about
the travellers meet more farm animals than vehicles
a man minding beasts gave them water
the writer announces a return worn out and changed
text: I am writing from an inn that clings to the side of a hill, where the wind beats at the shutters half the night. Let me set the trip down in pieces, the way it comes back to me. The room first: bare walls, a hard bed, a huge window that opens onto a dry, empty plateau. The food next: warm flatbreads, a goat's cheese so salty it stings the tongue, and a bitter brew the landlady pours into chipped bowls. Then the walking: we set off at sunrise along tracks that wind and double back, and we meet far more flocks than vehicles. One last heading, the people we came across: a man minding his beasts gave us water, and a village teacher told us the story of her hamlet. Nothing here looks like what I pictured before leaving. I shall come home browned by the sun, worn out, and probably a little altered.

units: the walker set off alone to empty his mind
he missed his first public transport
he waited under a metal shelter
he finished his journey by getting into passing vehicles
he slept behind an embankment to keep out of the wind
he strung a sheet of canvas between two posts as a shelter
the night was freezing but the clear sky kept him from sleeping
a storm turned the track to mud on the way back
he had to turn round and go back to the village
he would do it again with better equipment
text: So what possessed you to head off alone across that plateau? One sentence covers it: I wanted to walk until my head had emptied itself. And the start, did that go smoothly? Not at all. I missed the first bus, sat waiting under a tin shelter, and ended up crossing the plain in whatever passing vans would take me on board. Where did you sleep, then? Behind an embankment, out of reach of the gusts, with a sheet of canvas strung between two posts. Was the night rough? Freezing, yes, but the sky was so clear that I gave up on sleeping altogether. And coming back? That was where it went wrong: a storm turned the track to running mud, and I had to double back as far as the village. Would you do it again? Without a second thought, but with a proper tent and boots that grip on loose stone.

units: the warden of a mountain refuge describes the collapse of a path
the rain fell without a break and the stream swelled
a slope stripped of its trees no longer soaked up the water
the bank broke away after a sound of tearing
a small group of walkers stayed trapped above the break
the rescuers reached them by way of the ridge line
the walkers were led along a narrow, steep passage
no casualty was reported
the footbridge is destroyed for good
the local authorities are considering a new line higher up
text: The warden of a refuge high in the mountains tells of the night the path gave way. “The rain came down without a break, and the stream doubled in size,” he says. The cause is easy enough to pin down: a slope stripped of its trees held nothing back, and the water ran off in one unbroken sheet towards the track. “We heard something tear away, and then the bank went,” he goes on. The result was immediate. A handful of walkers found themselves trapped above the break, with no way down to the valley floor. A rescue team reached them along the ridge and led them out over a narrow, steep ledge. “Nobody was hurt, but the footbridge is lost for good,” he concludes. The valley council are already looking at a replacement line, higher up and well clear of the channel the water has carved.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: crossing a mountain range was once a risky undertaking
trains of pack animals went through snowbound gorges
even experienced guides lost their bearings
the difficulty came from the lack of visible landmarks
mist wiped out the shapes of the land
piles of stone were knocked over by the wind
wooden poles driven into the ground rotted in the damp
in the end notches were cut into the rock face and whitened
these notches stayed visible in spite of fresh snow
present-day waymarking systems descend from that invention
text: Crossing a mountain range was once a gamble with poor odds. Trains of pack animals pushed into gorges where snow wiped out the trail, and even seasoned guides lost their bearings between two slopes that looked alike. The difficulty lay not in the distance but in having nothing fixed to steer by once the mist swallowed the shapes of the land. Piles of stone were tried first, raised at intervals, and the wind knocked them over. Wooden poles came next, and the damp rotted them through. The answer arrived as a modest idea: cut a notch into the rock face at head height, then whiten it with lime, so that it showed even under fresh snow. The mule drivers could work their way from one notch to the next, with no need to read a sky that told them nothing. The waymarking systems in use now all descend from that invention.

units: a valley shaped by ice differs from a valley shaped by a river
the glacial valley has a broad, level floor
the walls of a glacial valley are almost vertical
the mass of ice wears away the base as much as the sides
the river valley forms a narrow, deep cut
water eats away mainly along the line it follows
the stones carried by the current grind the rock like an abrasive tool
the side valleys of a former glacier arrive high up
the side valleys of a river meet the main channel at the same level
text: A valley carved out by ice and a valley carved out by running water can be told apart at a glance. The glacial one has a broad, level floor between walls that rise almost straight up, because a thick, heavy mass of ice scrapes away at the base and the sides alike. The river valley cuts a narrow, deep groove instead, since water bites mainly along the line it follows and leaves the slopes to fall in under their own weight. The stones the current drags with it grind at the rock like a file. The side valleys give the difference away as well. Those of an old glacial valley arrive high up, left hanging, and spill down as waterfalls. Those of a river valley meet the main channel at the same level. That one detail is often enough to settle the question in front of a landscape you do not know.

units: the narrator reports a crossing he remembers precisely
the landscape was stony and had no tall plants
the swells of the ground fooled the eye about distance
the journey counted seven stages begun before sunrise
a halt took place in the shade during the greatest heat
the water came from built cisterns that the guides could find
the food was limited to hard flatbreads and a store of salt
a strap snapped and one of the party hurt a foot
a train of traders was coming the other way and reported a blocked well
the narrator concludes that bare ground holds many readable signs
text: One crossing has stayed sharp in my memory, and it is worth setting out its parts one by one. The setting: a desert of stone, no tall plant anywhere, rippled by swells of ground that fooled the eye about distance. The marching: seven stages, each begun before sunrise and closed at dusk, with a halt in the shade of a boulder through the worst of the heat. The supplies: water drawn from built cisterns that our guides found without hesitating, hard flatbreads, and a store of salt. The mishaps: a strap snapped, a foot cut open, a night when the wind flattened our shelter. The encounters, last of all: a train of traders working the same track the other way, who warned us of a well filled in with rubble. What I take from it is that bare ground is not empty, and reads like a crowded page.

units: the pack must be got ready the evening before departure

the water bottles are filled before leaving the hamlet
the route must be checked on the map before setting off
the springs and the steep sections must be located
regular stops serve to air and dry the feet

text: Pack your rucksack the evening before you leave, never at the last minute. Start by laying everything out flat on the floor: you will see at once what is missing and what is nothing but dead weight. Load the heavy items against your back, halfway up, so that the pull does not drag your shoulders backwards. Slip your rain jacket right at the top, where you can grab hold of it. Next morning, before you walk out of the hamlet, fill your bottles and check the line on the map, marking the springs and the steep sections. On the way, stop at regular intervals, take your boots off and let your feet dry properly. Choose your pitch for the night while it is still light, on a dry shelf of ground, well away from stream beds. When you wake, rub out every mark of your fire before you shoulder the pack again.

units: the number of walkers on a plateau path rose after it spread online
the village car park is full very early
meadows are being used as parking space
fences give way and the livestock escapes
the widening of the passage has destroyed the plant cover
rain now cuts grooves down the slope
the council is putting a shared shuttle in place
the number of spaces available is now limited
the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass recover
the shopkeepers protest while the stock farmers approve
text: It was meant to be a quiet season, and it has turned into a headache for the valley. Since the plateau path started doing the rounds online, walker numbers have shot up and the car park fills before the sun is properly over the ridge. Meadows are serving as parking space, fences give way, and the stock farmers watch their animals wander off. Naming the cause is easy; living with what follows is not. As boots have widened the passage, the plants that bound the soil have gone, and rain now cuts grooves down the slope. So the council has acted. A shuttle takes the place of cars, the number of spaces has been capped, and the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass recover. The shopkeepers grumble, the stock farmers breathe again, and the valley waits for the next season.
